practice_questions.marks: A word that imitates the natural sound of the thing it describes (1 mark). Accept examples such as 'crash,' 'hiss,' 'buzz' if accompanied by a brief definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a writer could use the sense of sound to create atmosphere in a descriptive piece.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each way described, up to 2 marks. For example: • Use onomatopoeia such as 'crash' or 'hiss' to make the reader hear the sound directly (1 mark). • Use a contrast between silence and sudden noise to create tension or surprise (1 mark). • Use repetition of sounds (e.g. 'yip yip yip') to convey a relentless or overwhelming atmosphere (1 mark). Accept any two valid methods with brief explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the 'zooming in' technique can help a student organise a descriptive writing response effectively.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation that covers: • Definition: zooming in means moving from a wide overview of a scene to a small, specific detail (1 mark). • Effect on reader: it mimics how the human eye works, creating a sense of discovery as focus narrows (1 mark). • Structural benefit: it provides a logical, deliberate organisation rather than random listing of details (1 mark). • Link to assessment: examiners reward 'varied and inventive use of structural features' at the highest band for content and organisation (1 mark). Accept reverse zoom (close to wide) if clearly explained.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Peter Fleming uses personification to describe the train crash in Source A. Use specific examples from the text to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks across two levels:
Upper band (4-6): Clear, detailed explanation with specific examples and analysis of effect. For example:
• The train 'sprawled foolishly' — the adverb 'foolishly' gives the train a human quality of embarrassment or stupidity, creating dark humour from the wreckage (up to 2 marks).
• The carriages are 'disposed in attitudes' and the last one remains 'primly, on the rails' — 'primly' suggests prim, proper behaviour, as if the carriage is morally superior to the others, adding absurdist comedy (up to 2 marks).
• The engine has 'a defiant and naughty look' and is 'definitely conscious of indiscretion' — it is presented as a mischievous child who knows it has done wrong, which undercuts the danger of the crash with comic tone (up to 2 marks).
Lower band (1-3): Some relevant examples identified with simple or partial explanation of effect.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following student response to a descriptive writing task:

'The beach was nice. The sea was blue and the sand was golden. There were some seagulls flying around. The sun was warm and it felt relaxing. I could hear the waves.'

Evaluate this response against the Level 4 descriptors for content and organisation. To what extent does it meet the standard? What specific improvements would you recommend?
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks using a three-level structure:
Top band (7-9): Perceptive evaluation that identifies specific weaknesses and offers detailed, practical improvements. The response should note:
• The writing tells rather than shows — 'The beach was nice' is a statement, not a description. Level 4 requires 'convincing and compelling' communication.
• Vocabulary is generic ('nice,' 'blue,' 'golden,' 'warm') — Level 4 requires 'extensive and ambitious vocabulary.'
• Only two senses are used (sight and touch/hearing briefly) and none are developed with figurative language.
• No structural variety — every sentence follows the same subject-verb-complement pattern.
• Improvements: use specific sensory detail ('the gritty warmth of sand between my toes'), figurative language ('waves exhaling against the shore'), varied sentence forms, and a deliberate structure (e.g. zooming in).
Mid band (4-6): Clear identification of some weaknesses with some useful suggestions.
Lower band (1-3): Simple or limited comments, may identify it as 'not very good' without specific analysis.

practice_questions.text:
You are going to enter a creative writing competition. Your entry will be judged by a panel of English teachers.

Write a description suggested by this task: 'Describe a place where everything has stopped.'

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)

Plan and write your response. You should aim to use precise sensory detail, varied sentence structures, and at least one example of the 'zooming in' technique.
practice_questions.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Communication is convincing and compelling. Tone, style and register assuredly matched to purpose. Extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices. Varied and inventive structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Communication is consistently clear. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect. Effective structural features. Coherent paragraphs with integrated discourse markers.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success. Conscious use of vocabulary. Some structural features. Some use of paragraphs.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication. Simple vocabulary. Limited structural features.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms for effect. High-level spelling including ambitious vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation range. Attempts variety of sentence forms.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Simple sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

Indicative content: Students should demonstrate careful observation of a still or frozen scene using multiple senses. Strong responses will use zooming in/out, figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification), varied sentence lengths for pace control, and ambitious vocabulary. The 'stopped' prompt lends itself to contrasts between stillness and implied movement, silence and implied sound.

before.exam_tip_html: In Question 5, examiners are looking for deliberate crafting — not a checklist of techniques. Do not try to cram every device you know into your response. Instead, choose three or four devices that suit your audience and form, and use them with purpose. A well-placed rhetorical question followed by a powerful tricolon will impress far more than ten devices used clumsily. Remember: the mark scheme rewards “sustained crafting of linguistic devices” at Level 4. The word “sustained” means consistent quality throughout, not one brilliant sentence surrounded by flat writing. Plan which devices you will use in your introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion before you start writing.

In Paper 1, Section B, examiners are looking for “sustained crafting of linguistic devices” to reach Level 4. A common mistake is to use sensory language in the opening paragraph and then forget about it. Make a conscious effort to weave sensory detail, powerful verbs and “show don’t tell” throughout your entire response — not just at the start. Before you begin writing, quickly note down one detail for each sense (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) related to your scenario. This takes 30 seconds and transforms the quality of your writing. Also, avoid naming emotions directly. Every time you catch yourself writing “I felt scared” or “she was angry,” stop and replace it with a physical reaction or sensory detail that shows the emotion instead.

In Paper 1 Question 5, examiners reward quality over quantity when it comes to figurative language. The Level 4 descriptor says “extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices.” The word “crafting” is key — it means your similes and metaphors should feel deliberate and purposeful, not thrown in randomly. Aim for two or three strong figurative moments across your whole response. Before writing a simile, ask yourself: does this create an image, match the mood, AND reveal something about the narrator or character? If it does all three, keep it. If it only does one, rethink it. And never, ever use a cliché — it signals to the examiner that you are writing on autopilot.

When you spot a rhetorical device in a Paper 2 source, always ask three questions: (1) What is the device? (2) What effect does it have on the reader? (3) Why did the writer choose this device here? Answering all three moves you from identification (Level 1) to analysis (Level 3–4). In Question 3, focus on how the device creates meaning within the specified lines. In Question 4, compare how two writers use similar or different devices to convey contrasting perspectives. Remember: the mark scheme rewards quality over quantity — three well-analysed devices will outscore six that are merely named.

In the Paper 1 creative writing question, spend 5 minutes planning your structure before you write a single sentence. Jot down which structural moves you will use in each paragraph (D, S, Z, L). Examiners can tell the difference between writing that was planned and writing that was made up as it went along. A clear, purposeful structure is the fastest way to move from Level 2 into Level 3 or Level 4 on AO5. Remember: the mark scheme rewards “varied and inventive use of structural features” at the top level — so use at least two or three of the four moves in every response.

Before you write a single word of your Question 5 response, identify PAFT (Purpose, Audience, Form, Topic), decide your position, and jot down 3–4 points in order of strength. Plan your opening hook and closing image. This takes 5 minutes and transforms a meandering response into a controlled, convincing argument. The mark scheme rewards “varied and inventive structural features” and “seamlessly integrated discourse markers” at Level 4 — both of which are virtually impossible without a plan. Remember: if you do not address the focus of the task, your AO5 mark is capped at 12 out of 24.

In AQA Paper 1 Question 5, examiners reward deliberate structural choices just as much as beautiful language. If you use a countdown narrative, make the time pressure visible to the reader — mention a clock, use temporal markers (“Ten minutes,” “Five,” “One”), or show time through changing light or sound. This signals to the examiner that your structure is intentional, not accidental, which is the difference between Level 3 (“controlled pace”) and Level 4 (“subtle variation of pace”). Always plan your five stages before you write, and always leave 5 minutes to proofread for AO6 — those 16 marks for technical accuracy are the easiest to improve on the day.

Q4 is the only reading question that asks for your personal response. The command phrase “to what extent do you agree” means you must state your position. Do not sit on the fence without ever committing — use phrases like “I strongly agree” or “I partially agree” to anchor each paragraph. The examiner is looking for a critical voice, not a neutral summary. Remember: always refer back to the exact words in the statement, always stay within the specified lines, and always explain the effect of methods on the reader. Quality beats quantity — three perceptive paragraphs will outscore five simple ones every time.

In Question 5, the examiner is looking for two separate things: your ideas and how accurately you write. Treat them as two separate challenges. When planning, focus entirely on what you want to say and how to structure it. When proofreading, focus entirely on technical accuracy — full stops, commas, spelling, homophones. Many students lose marks on AO6 not because they cannot spell, but because they rush and do not check. Remember: if you do not write in the correct form (e.g. you write a letter when asked for a speech), your content mark is capped at Level 2 (12 out of 24). Always underline the form, purpose and audience in the question before you begin.

In Paper 2 Section A, the most common reason students lose marks is poor time management — they spend too long on Q1 and Q2, then rush Q3 and Q4 which are worth the most marks. Stick to the timing plan: 5 minutes for Q1, 10 for Q2, 12 for Q3, and 18 for Q4. For Q3, remember the command word is “How” — this means analyse the effects of language, not describe what happens. For Q4, always use comparative connectives (“In contrast,” “Similarly,” “Whereas”) and write about methods as well as feelings. The mark scheme rewards “like-for-like” comparisons — if you discuss personification in Source A, compare it to personification (or another method) in Source B within the same paragraph.
